chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
Investing in a first income property is one of the best ways to build wealth in Quebec. But a plex is not a house: you buy it like a business, with numbers, not with your heart.

This guide gives you the basics: how to evaluate a building, calculate its profitability, finance it, and avoid the classic first-time investor mistakes.

Each chapter ends with a lined « My notes » page.

chapters.title: Think like an investor
chapters.objective: Adopt the business logic of rental real estate.
chapters.html:
Adopt the business logic of rental real estate.

An income property is judged on its numbers: rental income, expenses, financing, and the cash flow that is left over. You don't buy a plex because it's pretty, but because its numbers hold up.

  • Income: current and potential rents.
  • Expenses: taxes, insurance, maintenance, management, vacancy, bad debt.
  • Financing: down payment, mortgage payments.
  • Cash flow: what is left once everything is paid.
Emilie's tip

Fall in love with the numbers, not the bricks. An ordinary building with solid numbers is a far better investment than a beautiful plex that loses money every month.

chapters.title: Evaluate a building before making an offer
chapters.objective: Carry out the checks specific to rental property.
chapters.html:
Carry out the checks specific to rental property.

  • Analyze the leases, current rents vs the market, and the payment history.
  • Check the condition of the building (roof, structure, plumbing, electrical): repairs across several units are expensive.
  • Obtain the actual expenses (taxes, insurance, common-area energy, maintenance).
  • Factor vacancy and bad debt into the projections.

In Quebec, remember: leases run with the building. You inherit the tenants and their terms.

Emilie's tip

Demand the real numbers (leases, expenses, invoices), not the seller's optimistic projections. A building is bought on verified data, not on promises.

chapters.title: The classic first-time investor mistakes
chapters.html:
Avoid the most common pitfalls.

  • Overestimating income and underestimating expenses.
  • Forgetting vacancy, management, and the reserve for major work.
  • Assuming you can easily raise rents or evict tenants (the rules are strict).
  • Neglecting the inspection: a building hides more systems than a house.

A good project stays profitable even with a vacancy and a major repair in the same year. If it only works in the perfect scenario, it is too risky.

Emilie's tip

Build your numbers conservatively: realistic rents, complete expenses, a cushion for the unexpected. The seller's « on paper » profitability is almost always rosier than reality.

chapters.title: From analysis to offer
chapters.html:
Structure an investor's offer.

Once the numbers are validated, make a conditional offer: inspection, financing, and review of the leases and documents. These conditions protect you if the actual numbers differ from what was advertised.

The first building is a school: well chosen and well managed, it partly finances your learning curve and opens the door to the second.

Emilie's tip

Always have the leases and expenses reviewed BEFORE your conditions expire. Discovering an inflated rent or a hidden expense after the purchase is too late.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, in concrete terms.

This week

  1. Define my budget and my investor borrowing capacity.
  2. Learn to read a building's leases and expenses.

Within 30 days

  1. Analyze 2-3 buildings on their real numbers.
  2. Make a conditional offer on the best file.

Then

  1. Have the property inspected and validate the leases before removing my conditions.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Cash flow: the money left over after all expenses and financing.
  • Leases: contracts that run with the building in Quebec.
  • Vacancy: periods without a tenant to budget for.
  • Bad debt: unpaid rent to plan for.
  • Repair reserve: a provision for major repairs.
